passage:
After school the children lined up on the dusty ground behind the temple for kabaddi. Nikita and Sai were captains. One by one, names were called. Ravi. Pappu. Even little Sonu, who always cried when he was tagged.
Gautam stood on one leg, then the other, pretending to fix his slipper strap.
'Okay, that's even,' Nikita said, and the game began.
Gautam walked to the peepal tree and sat on its root. His throat felt tight and hot. He picked at a scab on his knee and watched the others shout and tumble in the dust. When his mother called him home, he said he had a stomach ache and went straight to bed without eating his rotis.

qa.q: Who were the captains?
qa.a: Nikita and Sai were the captains.

qa.q: Why did Gautam say he had a stomach ache?
qa.a: Gautam was hurt at being left out and didn't have words for it, so a stomach ache was easier to say than the real ache.

qa.q: What small step could Gautam's mother take at this stage?
qa.a: She could notice the uneaten rotis, sit with him and gently ask about his afternoon, offering words like 'left out' without rushing to fix it.

qa.q: What might Nikita have been thinking when saying 'that's even'?
qa.a: Nikita was probably thinking only about fair team numbers and may not have noticed Gautam standing there at all.

grounding: It shows a child left unpicked for a game who feels a sharp, personal hurt but cannot put it into words.

passage:
On Friday morning Mei came into class with a stack of pink envelopes. She walked between the desks, handing them out. 'For my party on Saturday!'
Valentina sat up straight and smoothed her skirt.
Mei put an envelope on Lucia's desk, then on Sam's, then walked right past.
Valentina looked down at her pencil case. She counted the pencils. Seven. She counted them again.
At break the others talked about the bouncy castle. Valentina stayed by the coat hooks, zipping and unzipping her jacket.
That evening her abuela asked about school. 'Fine,' Valentina said, and pushed her empanadas around the plate. Later, in bed, she cried quietly into her pillow, and when her abuela looked in, she couldn't say what was wrong.

qa.q: How many pencils did Valentina count?
qa.a: Valentina counted seven pencils.

qa.q: What does Valentina counting her pencils twice suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was trying to hold in a sharp hurt and hide it, giving her eyes and hands something else to do 😢

qa.q: How could Valentina's abuela support her at this stage?
qa.a: She could sit on the bed, say it looks like a sad day, and let Valentina talk or simply be held, without pushing for an explanation.

qa.q: What might Mei be experiencing while handing out the envelopes?
qa.a: Mei is probably excited about her party and focused on her own list, likely unaware how much it hurt to be passed by.

grounding: It shows a child left out of a birthday invitation who feels a big, personal ache she cannot explain.

passage:
On the dusty ground behind the panchayat office, the big children were picking teams for kabaddi. Zeenat, the tallest girl in Class 5, called names one by one. Ramu. Babloo. Chotu. Even the new boy from the ration shop.
Darshan stood on his toes. He had practised his raid breath all week, "kabaddi, kabaddi", under his blanket at night.
The teams were full. Nobody said his name.
Darshan's chest hurt, a sharp ache like when he fell off the wall. He picked up a stone and turned it over and over in his hand. When his grandmother called from the doorway, he said he wasn't hungry. That night he lay on his mat and didn't practise his raid breath. He didn't know how to tell anyone what was wrong.

qa.q: Who called the names for the teams?
qa.a: Zeenat, the tallest girl in Class 5.

qa.q: What does Darshan turning the stone over and over suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: He felt hurt and left out, a sharp ache he had no words to explain.

qa.q: What could his grandmother do to help Darshan tonight?
qa.a: Sit beside him on the mat, gently notice he seems sad, and let him tell her about the game when he's ready.

qa.q: How might Zeenat have seen the team picking?
qa.a: Zeenat may not have noticed Darshan at all, busy choosing the bigger children, with no idea how much it hurt.

grounding: A village boy left out of a team game feels a sharp ache of not belonging that he cannot put into words.

passage:
On Friday in the classroom in Oslo, Tomas handed out small blue envelopes with a rocket on each one. "For my birthday party," he said. Fatima watched the envelopes go down her row: Ella, Jonas, Sara. Then Tomas walked past her desk to the next row.
She looked down at her pencil case and pretended to be busy. Her cheeks felt hot and her throat went tight.
At lunch everyone talked about the bouncy castle. Fatima ate her sandwich very slowly and said nothing.
At home her mother asked about school. "Fine," Fatima said, and went to her room. She took out her drawing book and drew a rocket, then scribbled over it hard until the page tore. She didn't know why she felt so angry and sad at the same time.

qa.q: What was on each of Tomas's envelopes?
qa.a: A rocket.

qa.q: Why did Fatima scribble over the rocket until the page tore?
qa.a: She felt hurt and left out, and angry and sad at once, without words to explain it.

qa.q: How could Fatima's mother gently help?
qa.a: Sit with her, notice the torn drawing kindly and ask about the day quietly, so Fatima can name the hurt.

qa.q: What might Tomas have been thinking when he handed out the envelopes?
qa.a: Tomas may have had only a few invitations and not realised how being skipped would feel to Fatima.

grounding: A girl left out of a birthday invitation feels a hot, tight hurt of not belonging that she cannot name.

passage:
In the PE period at St Anne's School, Thomas was cricket captain. He picked fast, pointing: "You, you and you." Varun waited near the boundary rope with his hands behind his back.
"We've got enough," Thomas said, and ran to the pitch.
The PE teacher was busy with the other class. Varun sat on the steps near the water cooler. From there he could hear the bat hitting the ball and everyone shouting. Last year he and Thomas had been bowling partners.
His stomach felt heavy, like after eating too much, but it wasn't food. He pulled at a loose thread on his sock until it came out.
When the bell rang, a classmate asked why he hadn't played. "Didn't feel like it," Varun said, looking away.

qa.q: Where did Varun sit after not being picked?
qa.a: On the steps near the water cooler.

qa.q: What does Varun's heavy stomach show about how he felt?
qa.a: He felt hurt and left out, a heavy ache he couldn't explain, especially because Thomas used to be his bowling partner.

qa.q: What could the PE teacher do next time?
qa.a: Notice who is left out, check on Varun, and use a fairer way of picking teams so no child is skipped.

qa.q: What might Thomas be thinking as he runs to the pitch?
qa.a: Thomas is probably focused on the game and may not realise how hurt his old bowling partner is.

grounding: A boy not picked for a team feels a heavy ache of not belonging and hides it behind 'didn't feel like it'.

passage:
Monday: Aparna carried the drawing she had made for Charu's birthday all morning in her bag, a cat with a crown. She kept touching it through the zip.
Wednesday: at lunch, Charu gave out small blue cards to six girls in the class. Aparna waited with her hand half open. The last card went to the girl behind her. Aparna looked hard at her tiffin and ate every grain of rice, very slowly.
Friday: at home she didn't want to watch cartoons. When Amma asked what was wrong, she said, "My tummy hurts," and then, "Nothing." At bedtime she took the cat drawing out of her bag, folded it very small, and pushed it under her pillow.

qa.q: How many girls got blue cards from Charu?
qa.a: Charu gave small blue cards to six girls in the class.

qa.q: How can you tell Aparna felt hurt even though she said nothing?
qa.a: She stared at her tiffin and ate very slowly, then said her tummy hurt, which suggests a sharp, lonely ache she has no words for.

qa.q: How could Amma support Aparna at this stage?
qa.a: Amma could sit with Aparna, say it sounds like something sad happened, and gently ask about school without pushing, so Aparna can find words for being left out.

qa.q: How might Charu see the birthday cards?
qa.a: Charu may simply have had only a few cards to give and not noticed who was waiting, with no idea how much it hurt Aparna.

grounding: Shows a child left out of a birthday invitation feeling a big, personal hurt she cannot put into words.
